paras: The Greenville, North Carolina, police shooting of 1920 was an incident in which Lester Jones, chief of police in Greenville, N. C., fired into an automobile carrying four Black people when its driver did not stop at his order to halt. Two of the occupants were injured, and the chief's stated reason was that he "supposed" the car contained liquor. The shooting was reported by the Associated Negro Press and carried in the Savannah Tribune.

According to a dispatch datelined Greenville, July 28, 1920, Chief Jones called on the driver of a passing automobile to halt. When the driver failed to stop, Jones fired into the car, which held four "Colored people." Two of them were injured; the dispatch did not name them, describe their wounds, or say whether any liquor was found.
No report of an arrest, inquiry or charge against the chief or the occupants appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Tribune printed the item on August 7, 1920, under the headline "Police Chief Fires on Passing Automobile," as one of several Associated Negro Press briefs on its second page. The brief set the chief's justification in quotation marks, presenting the liquor suspicion as his supposition rather than as fact. It ran alongside items reporting a large exodus of Black residents from Vicksburg and a Memphis dispatch attributing migration north to lynching and "a general state of unrest." No white-press account of the shooting was found.
